explanations.explanation: Canaanites, friend. God says, "Your origin and your birth were in the land of the Canaanites." That's where Jerusalem's story starts. I think God starts there so we can see how far He takes her from that spot.

The Edomites are another people, friend, and they're not on this family tree. God says Jerusalem's origin and birth were in the land of the Canaanites. Her father was an Amorite and her mother a Hittite. No Edomites anywhere in that lineup.

The Moabites are a different people, friend. Verse 3 puts Jerusalem's origin and birth in the land of the Canaanites. Her father is an Amorite and her mother is a Hittite. Moab doesn't show up in that verse at all.
Zero, friend. No cord cut, no washing, no salt rub, no cloths. God says no one cared enough to do even one of these things out of compassion. That's a whole list of care, and she got none of it.

Not even one, friend. God says, "No one cared enough for you to do even one of these things out of compassion for you." The cord, the washing, the salt and the cloths all got skipped. I'd love to give her a partial score, but the text says zero.

That's the care she was supposed to get, friend, but nobody gave it. God says the cord wasn't cut, she wasn't washed, she wasn't rubbed with salt and she wasn't wrapped in cloths. Not one of the four happened. No one cared enough to do even one of them.
True. God says she was "thrown out into the open field, because you were despised on the day of your birth." That's a heavy beginning for anybody. I think this is where the story hurts most.

It's true, friend, and I wish it weren't. God says, "you were thrown out into the open field, because you were despised on the day of your birth." Nobody cared enough to keep her. That's a heavy part, so let's sit with it a second.
That's it, friend. God says, "as you lay there in your blood I said to you, 'Live!'" Then He says it again. He sees her in the worst spot and speaks life over her.
He doesn't, friend. He passes by, sees her, and stops with a word for her. He says, "Live!" Then He says it a second time.

explanations.answer: He sends her back to her parents
explanations.explanation: The text never says that, friend. God sees her lying in her blood and says to her, "Live!" Then He makes her thrive like a plant of the field. Her parents never come up again.
Not yet, friend. Verse 7 says she was grown up and very beautiful, "but you were naked and bare." The clothes come later, once God covers her. She hasn't gotten dressed up at this point.
False, and you caught it. She's grown and very beautiful, but God says she was "naked and bare." The fine clothes don't show up until verse 10. First comes the cloak.

explanations.answer: He enters into a covenant with her
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, "I pledged Myself to you, entered into a covenant with you, and you became Mine." It's a promise, and He's the one making it. She goes from the open field to belonging to Him.

explanations.answer: He hires her as His servant
explanations.explanation: No hiring happens, friend. God spreads His cloak over her and pledges Himself to her. Then He enters into a covenant with her, and He says, "you became Mine." That's a bond, not a job.

explanations.answer: He sends her back to her people
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. God pledges Himself to her and enters into a covenant with her. Then He says she became His. She isn't going anywhere.

A crown, friend. God says, "I put a ring in your nose, earrings on your ears, and a beautiful crown upon your head." He keeps adding to the outfit. Meanwhile my whole look is a hat, and I'm proud of that hat.
No helmet here, friend. This is a dress-up scene, not a battle scene. God puts a ring in her nose, earrings on her ears, and "a beautiful crown upon your head." Nothing in this list is for fighting.

The text doesn't mention a turban, friend. After the bracelets, the chain, the nose ring and the earrings, God puts "a beautiful crown upon your head." It's a crown, and that fits with her rising to be queen in verse 13.
Not a secret at all, friend. God says, "Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty." The nations heard about her. That news traveled.
False. God says, "Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty." It was no secret. The word got out far past her own front door.
Right. God says her beauty "was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you." It was a gift from Him. Keep that in your pocket, friend, because it matters for what comes next.
Her father shows up in verse 3, but he's not the source here. God says her beauty was perfect "in the splendor I bestowed on you." That splendor came from God. Dad doesn't get the credit.
The text points somewhere else, friend. God says her beauty "was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you." Bestowed means it was given to her. She didn't earn it.
True. God says, "because of your fame, you trusted in your beauty." The trouble starts when she looks at herself instead of at the One who gave it to her. That's the turn in the story, friend.
It's true, friend. God says, "But because of your fame, you trusted in your beauty and played the harlot." Her trust landed on her own beauty. That's where it all turns.
Idols, friend. God says, "You also took the fine jewelry of gold and silver I had given you, and you made male idols." The gifts He gave her became the very things she turned to. That's heavy.
No thrones here, friend. God says she took the gold and silver jewelry He gave her and made male idols. Her own gifts got turned into the idols.
No coins, friend. Verse 17 says she took the fine jewelry of gold and silver God had given her. She made male idols with it.

True. God says, "you set before them as a pleasing aroma the food I had given you—the fine flour, oil, and honey that I had fed you." Then He adds, "That is what happened." Even her meals went to the idols.

It's true, friend. God says she set before the idols "the food I had given you—the fine flour, oil, and honey that I had fed you." He had fed her that, and she set it in front of idols. He even says, "That is what happened."

explanations.answer: The days when she lay in her blood
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. God says, "you did not remember the days of your youth when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your own blood." She forgot where she came from. Forgetting her beginnings is a big part of this story.

explanations.answer: The songs she sang as a queen
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions any songs, friend. God says she did not remember "the days of your youth when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your own blood." That's what slipped her mind.

explanations.answer: The names of all her neighbors
explanations.explanation: No neighbor names in that verse, friend. God says she did not remember the days of her youth, "wallowing in your own blood." It was her own past she forgot, not a list of names.
The opposite, friend. God says she built a lofty shrine "in every public square" and "at the head of every street." Those are some of the busiest spots in town. Nothing about that was tucked away.

False, and you read it right. God says she "built yourself a mound and made yourself a lofty shrine in every public square." She built them at the head of every street too. These were out in the open for everyone to see.
The Egyptians, friend. God says, "You prostituted yourself with your lustful neighbors, the Egyptians." They're the first neighbor He names.
The Ammonites aren't named in this stretch, friend. God names "your lustful neighbors, the Egyptians" first. After them come the Assyrians and Chaldea.
The Arameans don't show up here, friend. The first neighbor God names is "the Egyptians." Then He names the Assyrians, and after that Chaldea.
They weren't impressed, friend. God says the daughters of the Philistines, who hate her, "were ashamed of your lewd conduct." Ashamed is the opposite of impressed. Even her enemies were embarrassed.
False. God says the daughters of the Philistines "were ashamed of your lewd conduct." These are people who hated her, and even they were ashamed. That tells you how far it went.

Right, friend. God says, "you were not yet satisfied. Even after that, you were still not satisfied." She keeps reaching and keeps coming up empty. It's like eating cookies and still wanting more, except these aren't cookies.
She never gets there, friend. God says she "was not yet satisfied. Even after that, you were still not satisfied." The Assyrians didn't fill that gap either.

That's not in this verse, friend. God says she turned to the Assyrians "because you were not yet satisfied." Then He adds that even after that, she was still not satisfied. Nothing in the text says she turned back.

explanations.answer: She pays her lovers to come to her
explanations.explanation: She does, friend. God says, "you gave gifts to all your lovers. You bribed them to come to you from everywhere." Then He says she paid a fee instead of receiving one. He calls it the opposite of other women.

explanations.answer: She demands gold and silver from them
explanations.explanation: It runs the other way, friend. God says, "you paid a fee instead of receiving one." She's the one handing out the gifts. She's paying them.

explanations.answer: She sends every one of them away
explanations.explanation: She does the opposite, friend. God says she bribed her lovers "to come to you from everywhere." She was drawing them in, and she paid them to come. Sending them away wasn't on her mind.
That's the one, friend. God says it's "because of the blood of your children which you gave to them." This is one of the heaviest parts of the whole passage. I think this one hurts.

Her birth isn't the reason God gives, friend. He says it's because she poured out her wealth, exposed her nakedness to her lovers and idols, "and because of the blood of your children which you gave to them." That last one is the one the question is after. It's a heavy one.

Harvests don't come up, friend. God lists what she poured out, and then He adds "the blood of your children which you gave to them." That's the reason the question wants. It's a heavy one, so let's take it seriously.

All of them, friend. God says, "I will surely gather all the lovers with whom you found pleasure, all those you loved and all those you hated." He gathers them from all around. The ones she turned to become the ones standing against her.
No angels in this verse, friend. God says He will gather "all the lovers with whom you found pleasure." He gathers them against her from all around.
Persia isn't mentioned here, friend. God says He will gather her lovers, "all those you loved and all those you hated." They're the ones He brings against her.
True. God says, "I will sentence you to the punishment of women who commit adultery and those who shed blood." Both are named. This is a heavy verse, so no jokes from me.
It's true, friend. God says, "I will sentence you to the punishment of women who commit adultery and those who shed blood." He names both. It's a heavy verse.
Down they go. God says her lovers "will level your mounds and tear down your lofty shrines." What she built up is what comes down. Nothing she built stays standing.
The opposite, friend. God says they "will level your mounds and tear down your lofty shrines." No extra floors are going on. They're coming down.
No guards here, friend. God says her lovers will level her mounds and tear down her lofty shrines. They aren't protecting anything.
Not in secret, friend. God says they will "execute judgment against you in the sight of many women." Many women will be watching, so it's out in the open.
False, and you got it. God says they will "execute judgment against you in the sight of many women." It's done where people can see.
Pay, friend. God says, "I will put an end to your prostitution, and you will never again pay your lovers." Remember the fee she kept handing out? That stops.
Not fear, friend. The verse says God will put an end to her prostitution, "and you will never again pay your lovers." The word is pay. That ties back to the fee she paid them earlier.
Not find, friend. God says, "I will put an end to your prostitution, and you will never again pay your lovers." The word is pay. She'd been the one paying the whole time.

That's not what verse 42 says, friend. God says, "So I will lay to rest My wrath against you, and My jealousy will turn away from you." Then He says, "Then I will be calm and no longer angry." His anger doesn't go on forever.

False, and that's good to hear. God says, "So I will lay to rest My wrath against you, and My jealousy will turn away from you. Then I will be calm and no longer angry." The anger is laid to rest. After a passage this heavy, that's a relief.
